q: Running the same code with the same seed gives the same 'random' numbers.
why: Fact. The generator is a fixed recipe: same seed, same sequence, like replaying a recorded shuffle.

o: the starting number for the generator's recipe
why: Change the seed and you get a different but equally random-looking sequence.

q: Which is the recommended way to get random numbers in modern numpy?
o: rng = np.random.default_rng(seed) and pass rng around
why: An explicit generator is isolated from other code's draws and repeatable.

q: Eight workers all use default_rng(1). What happens?
o: they repeat the same runs, so you have one worker's worth of data
why: Like four friends using one recorded list of coin flips: copies, not new data.

q: With 9 workers all using the same seed, by what factor is the reported standard error too small?
why: There is only 1/9 of the claimed data, so the true error is √9 = 3× the reported one.

q: How do you give 16 workers independent streams from one recorded number?
o: reuse one generator in every process
why: spawn derives independent child seeds from one parent seed.

q: Trying seeds until the new strategy wins, then reporting that run, is fine if the code is correct.
why: Myth. Choosing the seed by its result is cherry-picking, like p-hacking.

q: Common random numbers are like testing two running shoes …
o: in the same weather, so the weather cancels out
why: Both scenarios see the same random draws, so luck cancels in the difference.

q: Common random numbers cut the standard error of a difference from 1.03 to 0.40. About how many times more independent runs would match it?
why: Runs scale with the variance ratio: (1.03/0.40)² ≈ 6.6.

q: Simulation random numbers are suitable for passwords and security tokens.
why: False. Use the secrets module; simulation generators are predictable by design.
